title: Nicholas (6 December)
hookLine: a bishop who secretly gave dowries to three poor girls, the root of Santa Claus

cards: A bag of gold sails through an open window in the dark and lands on the floor of a poor man's house. Nobody sees who threw it.
The man has three daughters and no money for their dowries, and in that world, the story says, it meant they had no good future ahead of them. Now one of them can marry.
A while later, another bag comes through the window. Then the father decides he has to know. He waits up, and he catches a man at the window: Nicholas.

teach.b: Nicholas was a bishop of Myra, a town on the southern coast of what is now Turkey. Very little is known for certain about his life. What came down instead is a set of stories, and the dowry story is the one that stuck.
In the telling, Nicholas has inherited money and wants to help the family without being seen.

teach.h: THREE NIGHTS, AND THEN: TELL NO ONE.
teach.b: So he goes at night, three times. On the third night the father runs out and catches him, and falls at his feet. And Nicholas asks him for one thing: tell no one.
That request is the heart of it. Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount.

teach.h: LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." And the promise that follows: "thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee." Nicholas wanted the gift to be all gift.
There's a small irony here. The father clearly didn't keep the secret, or we'd never have heard it. And the secret giver ended up with a very public afterlife.
In the Netherlands he became Sinterklaas, and the usual account traces Santa Claus to that Dutch name.

teach.h: THY FATHER WHO SEETH IN SECRET.
teach.b: In parts of Europe, children still set out shoes on the eve of his feast and find small gifts in them by morning.
Under the red suit and the reindeer is a bishop at a window, throwing gold into the dark and hoping not to be seen.

how: Saint Nicholas is remembered on 6 December; in parts of Europe children set out shoes or stockings the night before and find small gifts in the morning, and some parishes collect gifts for the poor around his feast.

games.q: you're Nicholas. on the third night, as the last bag of gold goes through the window, the father runs out and catches you. what do you do?
o: tell him to thank the church
ask him to tell no one
run before he sees your face
games.why: in the story he asks the father to keep it secret. the father didn't, which is the only reason we know.

practice: Think of someone who could use a lift right now: not a grand gesture, but coffee paid for, a note left on a desk, a bill quietly covered, a chore done before anyone wakes up.
Choose one, work out how it could be done so they never find out it was you, and notice how it feels to give up the thank-you in advance. If you pray, offer the gift to God before you give it.

wordCard.voice: Nicholas. The bishop of Myra who threw dowries through a poor man's window at night, asked to stay unknown, and became the root of Santa Claus.

orig.note: Greek: Nicholas's name, as the Greek-speaking church of Myra wrote it.

carryVoice: Your line: in secret. A gift that's all gift, with no thank-you note coming back. Go gently.
